source.title: Differential roles of human striatum and amygdala in associative learning

confidence_rationale: Human aversive (shock) reversal learning: amygdala BOLD tracks model-derived Pearce-Hall associability, dissociated from striatal prediction error. The most direct support in the set for MECH-598 in the AVERSIVE domain and for its reversal signature. Model-based fMRI correlation rather than causal manipulation.
failure_signatures: Amygdala tracked associability while striatum tracked prediction error; a single system computing both the delta-rule update and the associability would not reproduce the dissociation.
The evidence is correlational model-based fMRI; associability being represented in amygdala does not show that it controls the learning rate causally.

mapping.source_claim_statement: In a human reversal learning task with aversive reinforcement, amygdala BOLD activity tracked associability as estimated by a hybrid Pearce-Hall/Rescorla-Wagner model, dissociated from the striatal representation of reinforcement prediction error.
mapping.ree_translation: Supports MECH-598 on the two points where the animal work is weakest: valence (aversive) and reversal (the claim's confirming criterion (ii) is faster re-learning after an A/B swap, the Pearce-Hall signature). It also supports the claim's separation of associability from the delta-rule update REE already has in harm regression readouts.
mapping.mapping_caveat: Associability here is a trial-wise scalar per cue in a simple two-cue design, fitted from skin conductance; it is not a retrospective eligibility window over many candidate causes. BOLD correlation, not causation. Human task with instructed-free shocks, far from an agent's self-state.
mapping.source_context: Human fMRI, Pavlovian reversal with mild shock, hybrid Pearce-Hall model fitted to SCR

confidence_components.notes: Nature Neuroscience brief communication, model-based, human, aversive. Mapping good for the associability-as-state-in-aversive-learning core; lower for the multi-candidate retrospective window.
